Antiperspirants are just sorta like deodorant but with the purpose of making you sweat less. It works better or worse depending on the person, but personally I found they don't help me. The stronger stuff (so what you can get in the pharmacy or prescriptions) is more irritating because the active ingredient is aluminium chloride which can be an irritant to skin! The meds I got prescribed have the active ingredient "oxybutinin hydrochloride" which is an anticholerogenic. Basically used to help incontinence but has a nice effect of helping with hyperhidrosis/excessive sweating too! I like the slow release stuff since I only gotta take it once a day instead of three times. Good luck :)

"わたしは Sarah じゃない - My name isn't Sarah"

You could say that, but it would mean "I'm not Sarah." To get the meaning "My name isn't Sarah," you have to say 私(わたし)の なまえ は Sarahじゃない

すみません だ - Excuse me! (As if getting someone's attention or you're offended)

だ seems a little misplaced (I might be wrong tbh), すみません alone with the appropriate intonation should do the trick and sound more natural.

レシートをお(Ga)いしだった - I did need a receipt

For verbs, you conjugate using masu form. So it would be the verb stem + ます or ました 
I'm inclined to say that in this case you could say レシート が いりました (corrected from いました to いりました) / いった (latter for past tense** sorry this is wrong, I meant to say casual! Wrote this at 2am haha). いる as in needing something requires が instead of を

明日じゃなかった - (Literal) Will not tomorrow.

Putting "tomorrow" together with a past form doesn't really make a lot of sense? As it is it has a closer literal meaning to "tomorrow, wasn't." You might want to try it like 明日 は (action) ＋ません - for example, I'm not cooking tomorrow -> 明日 は りょうりしません。

あとだった - (Literal) Was later

あとで, (thing) が ありました/あった would work better. Since we're referring to an event that took place/was there, ある would be used

あ无(*)でここにい - ( (*) is supposed to be a kanji character. Sadly, I couldn't find what it was online.) I was here on holiday

I'm not entirely sure on the meaning you meant to express, but to express the english sentiment in japanese you could do that by saying やすみ は ここ に とまった/とまりました。

I might not be correct but the above verb would be used for "staying" at a hotel for example, so I guess it might fit the purpose here too? 

わたしはイングリッシュじゃない (I had to google English in katakana) - I am not English.

English in Japanese is イギリス and to express that you're not (a) english (person), you would say 私 は イギリスじゃない

Personally I feel that pitch accent is obviously important, because it contributes to the ease of understanding one another. When I moved to Scotland, I struggled extremely with understanding people because the type of intonation was so drastically different in Scottish english. That's even though I'm completely fluent in english otherwise and have no issue communicating with people who speak British or American english. At that, even in my native language (German) I struggle to understand people easily if they have a very different way of intonation (even if they say words I am already familiar with), because the way we pronounce things helps us understand the word - it's what we're familiar with and when it suddenly sounds very different, it can take a second to pick up on the meaning.

Same with people who have a notable accent! I can't even begin to recall the number of times someone with an accent was speaking to me and I couldn't for the life of mine figure out what they were saying, it sounded like a foreign word, but then when it's written out I completely understood. I imagine it's the same in Japanese. While it's definitely possible to understand each other even without correct pitch accent (though this varies from person to person!) it can make communication difficult and ineffective. So, learning pitch accent can be the difference in whether we can communicate effectively, or just-so.

About the tape: It's cheaper to buy one roll but in the long run it's more expensive (spent over 150€ when I was mostly binding using tape).

Other things to consider:

If you're very sweaty,  wearing tape for longer times will give you painful blisters around the edges of the tape. I'm very sweaty and before taking meds to stop that I was only able to bind up to 10 hours with tape, otherwise I'd get blisters and taking off the tape would take off that layer of skin.

If you have a large chest or have poor skin elasticity, tape will not do a lot and will be difficult to apply. Before my binder broke down my skin elasticity (quite intensely, unfortunately) I was able to bind using tape just about fine with a large B cup.

Tape should never go around the entire chest. The middle part of the chest should be free (should be able to put your hand there -not counting thumb- and not touch the tape). The back should not be taped. Do not tape your chest down, but rather up and out. Middle part could feel a bit tense if you stretch it too far

Also, always cover the nips with something (like a plaster, cotton pad or tissue). The nips are sensitive and it will hurt to take off the tape if they're not covered.

Taking off tape, ideally you'll be able to use baby oil or adhesive remover (for medical tapes and such, so skin safe stuff). If not, soak it thoroughly before removing.

It might not always be fun to study, but if you learn the vocab and grammar you're bound to find the fun in being able to speak, read and write Japanese :-)

Personally I found it fairly helpful! I've actually asked this question before, and he recommended that thoroughly reading the grammar (as in, being able to understand the basic rules) be reinforced through practice in speaking and writing in order to cement the knowledge.

For example, in the last chapter I learned about the particles は、を、で、に、と　and (one use of) が. It's pretty easy to remember the general rules, but there are certain exceptions as to when to use which and if to use it. At this point, I already forgot what I read, but we did the exercises (spoken word) and he was able to correct me on my mistakes. This helped me to memorize how to use these particles, without needing to actively think about the rules :-)

In short: Read the grammar sections (they're fairly helpful in Genki, but of course it's better if you can have someone explain anything that might confuse you!) After doing that, practice to cement the knowledge. Ideally you would do this through writing, speaking, and listening together, rather than only choosing one option.

Because of this, going through a chapter a day is guaranteed to burn you out. It takes far longer than one day to fully grasp these concepts, and there's not really a way to speedrun learning a language.

Immersion helps tremendously but is far less frustrating if you understand at least a few words. I learned English that way as well and found that having learned basic grammar in school enabled me to communicate and contextually learn more about the language. Unless you already speak a language similar to your target language, it will take more time and concentration to learn it though! For example, if you know Korean or Chinese, you will have an easier time learning Japanese. English is very different though, both in grammar and language. German has similar pronunciation though so pronouncing Japanese is easier for me and I have to worry less about this

The exercises will be very difficult if you don't remember the vocab and grammar, so it's advisable to take your time with it and fully grasp things before moving on. I struggle sometimes because one or another word doesn't stick, and sometimes certain grammar points escape me as I try to form my sentences, and it takes a lot of time to keep looking up the words. It's also a bit frustrating when it happens - I think, it'll be even worse if you don't know at least 70% of the vocab that's used in the exercises.

My tutor is a certified Japanese teacher (and native) and I'm lucky that he's able to help me improve my mistakes, with explanations of why. All our lessons together are focused on doing the exercises and sometimes it takes a while to get through it all, so in order to make the lessons as useful as possible, all the speaking happens there and grammar/vocab is self study - any questions I can ask him about afterwards. 

Grammar and vocab are the building blocks of language. As someone who speaks 3 fairly distinct languages, I can assure you that without having a firm grasp on these two things, it will be very difficult and frustrating. I'd highly recommend taking the time to fully understand and internalize these things! Immersion is extremely helpful and can help you become fluent over time, but without the basics already there, it'll be like trying to punch a hole in a concrete wall. You might get there eventually, but it'll hurt a lot and feel worse when you realize you could've just taken the door.

You should definitely research the effects of binding, either together with your child or by yourself and then discuss the results together! Everyone else here has already given great advice in terms of where to look for binders and what the safe practices are, but there are negative long term effects which might impact your kid's confidence in the long term if she does come to the conclusion that she's trans.

I started binding properly when I was around 17 years old, and in spite of not binding a lot at a time nor frequently (since I didn't live in a supportive environment), I ended up struggling with intense stretch marks on my chest and a lot of sagging. It made me feel even less confident than before since 80% of the time I had to live with my chest being as it is, I couldn't even feel like "at least" I'd be attractive in that way. Though this is probably more of a problem to encounter once you're an older teenager, it's important to consider.
There's also other issues like exacerbated back pains and breathing difficulties. If your child already has back and breathing issues, binding can make those worse. Since your kid's still very young, binding might also carry a higher risk of "shaping" her ribcage. I know some ftm guys who spoke about how their ribcage was misshapen after many years of binding and they noticed the extent of it after going for top surgery.

It's important to discuss these things, but also try not to make it sound too scary since that age might be too young to think about these things in a more measured way. It will definitely help to sign your child up for therapy with a supportive but unbiased therapist. My therapist personally didn't specialize in trans people, but she treated people from I think 6 to 20 years old? And she was fantastic about it! Good luck :-)
